The XRI get/put lists were partitioned per hardware queue. However
adapter rarely had sufficient resources to give a large number of resources
per queue. As such
column2: it became common for a cpu to encounter a lack of XRI

column1: resource and request the upper io stack to retry after returning a BUSY
condition. This occurred even though other cpus were idle and not using
their resources.
Create as efficient a scheme as possible to move resources to the cpus that
need them. Each cpu maintains a small private pool which it allocates from
for io. There is a watermark that the cpu attempts to keep in the private
pool.  The private pool
column3: pulls from a global pool from the

column1: cpu. When the cpu's global pool is empty it will pull from other cpu's
global pool. As there many cpu global pools (1 per cpu or hardware queue
count) and as each cpu selects what cpu to pull from at different rates and
at different times
column2: it creates a radomizing effect that minimizes the

column1: number of cpu's that will contend with each other when the steal XRI's from
another cpu's global pool.
On io completion
column2: a cpu will push the XRI back on to its private pool.  A

column1: watermark level is maintained for the private pool such that when it is
exceeded it will move XRI's to the CPU global pool so that other cpu's may
allocate them.
On NVME
column2: as heartbeat commands are critical to get placed on the wire

column1: single expedite pool is maintained. When a heartbeat is to be sent
allocate an XRI from the expedite pool rather than the normal cpu
private/global pools. On any io completion
column2: if a reduction in the expedite

column1: pools is seen
column2: it will be replenished before the XRI is placed on the cpu

column1: private pool.
Statistics are added to aid understanding the XRI levels on each cpu and
their behaviors.
